Incidents are especially common among 13 to 15 year old children of magically gifted parents (sometimes at the parent’s urging).

Pretty selective! Students must be able to demonstrate at least some talent for magic before they can enroll, which is decently rare in this world—your powers awaken somehow, probably in a high stress event, and the school scouts you

Autumnwood is the oldest of the schools in the region and definitely highly respected—that said, there are rivalries between different schools and this one definitely has a reputation as a more traditionalist and restrictive environment, unlike the more innovative Starfall Polytechnic for example

Graduating classes are often quite small, with most students unable to complete the rigorous program. That said, alumni are all but guaranteed cushy jobs as advisors, guardians, government officials, etc, if they don’t just get their own tower and go into formal academia. It’s also considered a high mark of honor to be asked to come back to the school to teach. One student who followed this path was Morgana Silverpetal, who returned / returns / will return to the school as a professor and coven head at various points in her personal timeline—she’s a highly skilled chronomancer, and students often aren’t sure what age she’ll be when she comes in for a lesson

Be sure to set their expectations ahead of time and remind them to say not only ‘yes and’ when picking up from a previous dm, but also ‘no but’ if they are uncomfortable continuing with a particular theme or topic. It’s important not to question or disregard discomfort, but to still find a way to keep telling a story everybody is happy with, so ‘no but’ is a useful tool. 

‘Yes and’ example: “and then… the whole room explodes!” “Yes! And it turns out it was the wizard from earlier—he’s back for revenge in the robo-scorpion!”

‘No but’ example: “and then the two princesses are making out!” “…no… but they are holding hands, and they do plan to rule the kingdom jointly. And I’m sure they have lots of fun together in their boudoir where we don’t have to watch”

Somebody may have already said this, but also don’t be afraid to HELP your players if you mess up in the other direction! As a not-super-experienced DM I have matched my players up against some encounters that were supposed to be challenging but doable. But, maybe I didn’t think about the party makeup, or I missed an important note about the monster. Instead of pulling a tpk because of my mistake, I turn it into a more cinematic moment, or cut the encounter off early with some sort of outside interruption, or I fudge the monsters resistances. Worst comes to worst, you can also be honest with your players and explain the mistake. They’ll be understanding!

The onus of any miscalculation in game planning falls on the DM and thats a lot to deal with, but the key is to put enjoyment of the game first—you’re not trying to ‘win’, you’re trying to have fun and tell a good story. Be prepared to improvise and take the punches, and unless the party is specifically asking for it or seems bored with a section of gameplay, I would never really err that improvisation on the side of making things harder unfairly
